learning_objectives.en: Locate main ideas in two new texts, choose headings and justify them with the topic sentence.
learning_objectives.vi: Xác định ý chính hai bài mới, ghép heading và chỉ bằng chứng trong đoạn.

content.en: A heading must describe the whole paragraph. For an evidence question, locate which sentence proves the interpretation. The text may contain examples of other headings, but they are not dominant.
content.vi: Heading phản ánh toàn đoạn. Với câu bằng chứng, chỉ ra câu hỗ trợ; đoạn có thể nhắc chủ đề phụ nhưng không phải ý chính.

vocabulary.example_en: Summarise the main idea of the paragraph.
vocabulary.example_vi: Tóm tắt ý chính đoạn văn.

vocabulary.example_en: A statistic may be a supporting detail.
vocabulary.example_vi: Số liệu có thể là chi tiết hỗ trợ.

strategies.en: Summarise each paragraph in your own words before considering options; this limits vocabulary-matching traps.
strategies.vi: Tự tóm mỗi đoạn trước khi nhìn phương án để tránh bẫy từ giống.

common_mistakes.wrong: Paragraph C mentions museums, so heading: Museum history.
common_mistakes.correct: Paragraph C focuses on how cities spread tourists across time and space.

reason.en: Museums are only one example among several solutions.
reason.vi: Bảo tàng chỉ là một ví dụ trong nhiều giải pháp.

mini_review.en: Can you state one reason why each wrong heading is too narrow, too broad or unsupported?
mini_review.vi: Bạn giải thích được vì sao heading sai quá hẹp, quá rộng hay thiếu chứng cứ?

passages.title: A town that redesigned its station area
passages.text:
[A] Ten years ago, arriving at the railway station in the fictional town of Kelby was an unpleasant experience. Passengers stepped out into a large car park, crossed a busy road with no pedestrian crossing and walked past empty warehouses to reach the town centre. Local businesses complained that visitors left as soon as possible, and accident figures showed that the road outside the station was one of the most dangerous in the region.

[B] The first major change was to the bus station, which used to stand on the far side of the road, about two hundred metres from the trains. It has been moved directly in front of the station entrance, so that passengers can change from train to bus under a single roof. The number of bus routes stopping at the station has also increased from four to nine.

[C] The large car park to the east of the station has been reduced by half. In its place, a public square has been created, with trees, benches and a small café. A wide pedestrian crossing now connects the square to a footpath that runs along the canal to the town centre. A secure cycle store with space for two hundred bicycles has been built next to the ticket office.

[D] Three years after the work was completed, the results are mostly encouraging. The number of people walking from the station to the town centre has doubled, and there have been no serious accidents on the road since the crossing was installed. However, some residents of nearby villages say that it is now harder to find a parking space, and a park-and-ride service on the edge of town is still being planned.

[E] Planners from other towns have visited Kelby to learn from the project. The lesson they most often take away is that the order of the work mattered. The bus station was moved first, so that passengers already had a better connection before any parking spaces were removed. Had the car park been reduced first, the council believes, opposition would have been much stronger, and the rest of the scheme might never have been approved. The town is now consulting residents about extending the canal footpath to the hospital on the western edge of town.
passages.origin: Supplied independent English Skill Lab course corpus; not the book

passages.title: Why tourists crowd the same places
passages.text:
[A] In some of the world’s most famous destinations, residents now complain that their cities are being overwhelmed. Narrow streets are blocked by tour groups, rents rise as apartments are turned into holiday lets, and local shops are replaced by souvenir stores. The problem is not that tourism exists, but that very large numbers of visitors arrive in the same small areas at the same times.

[B] Part of the reason is the way places are now discovered. Before travelling, many people look at the same photographs online and want to stand in exactly the same spots. A single viewpoint can attract thousands of visitors a day, while a beautiful street a few minutes away remains almost empty. Travel guides that list the “top ten” sights of a city have a similar effect.

[C] Several cities are experimenting with ways to spread visitors more evenly. Some museums now require tickets to be booked for a particular time. Tourist offices promote lesser-known neighbourhoods and towns outside the city, and some have stopped printing maps that mark only the most famous sights. Others charge higher prices during the busiest months and offer discounts for visits in winter.

[D] The most successful plans, according to researchers, are those that involve residents from the start. In one coastal town, a committee of local people helped decide where tour buses could stop and which streets should be closed to groups. Because the rules were agreed locally, they were respected, and both residents and businesses reported improvements within two years.

[E] Tourists themselves can also make a difference. Travel writers increasingly encourage visitors to stay longer in one place instead of rushing between famous sights, to visit in spring or autumn rather than in midsummer, and to spend money in family-run businesses. Such choices may seem small, but in a city that receives millions of visitors a year, even a modest shift in behaviour can reduce crowding in the busiest streets. Some cities now publish live information showing how busy each major sight is, so that visitors can choose a quieter time.
